scenes.label: Session 5 · Agile
scenes.title: Agile project management
scenes.subtitle: The software development life cycle, Scrum, Kanban, and how to run it with Trello or Jira

beats.say: Welcome. Once you know what to build, you have to organise the work of building it. In this video: the software development life cycle, Scrum, Kanban, and two tools to run them, Trello and Jira.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.text: What users and the business need.

steps.title: Testing
steps.text: Verify it works and meets the need.

beats.say: Every software product, and most digital products, go through the same phases. This is the software development life cycle, or SDLC. Planning: goals, scope, budget and risks. Requirements: what users and the business need. Design: architecture, data and interfaces.
Implementation: writing and reviewing the code. Testing: checking that it works and meets the need. Deployment: releasing it to users. And maintenance: fixing, improving and operating it.
The phases are always there. The real question is how you go through them: once, in sequence, or many times, in short cycles.

scenes.label: Two ways through the cycle
scenes.title: Waterfall vs Agile
rows: One big release at the end

beats.say: In a waterfall project, you go through the phases once, in sequence. Requirements are fixed at the start, and users see the product at the end.

In an agile project, you go through all the phases in every short iteration, and deliver a working increment every one to four weeks. Change is expected, and risks appear early, when they are still cheap to fix.
Waterfall still works when the problem and the solution are well known, like building a bridge. When they are uncertain, like in a startup, agile wins.

scenes.label: Agile Manifesto · 2001
scenes.title: Four values of the Agile Manifesto
scenes.banner: The items on the right still matter. The items on the left matter more.

beats.say: In 2001, seventeen software developers met in Utah and wrote the Agile Manifesto. It has four values. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools. Working software over comprehensive documentation.
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation. And responding to change over following a plan.
Notice the word over. Processes, documents, contracts and plans still matter. The things on the left simply matter more.

scenes.label: 02 · Scrum
scenes.title: Scrum in one picture: 3 accountabilities, 5 events, 3 artifacts

cards.title: Events
cards.text: The sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective.

scenes.banner: Scrum is a lightweight framework: few rules, built on transparency, inspection and adaptation.

beats.say: Scrum is the most widely used agile framework. You can summarise it in three numbers. Three accountabilities: the product owner, who maximises value and orders the backlog; the scrum master, who makes Scrum work; and the developers, who build.
Five events: the sprint itself, sprint planning, the daily scrum, the sprint review and the sprint retrospective.
And three artifacts: the product backlog, the sprint backlog and the increment.
Scrum is deliberately lightweight. It rests on three pillars: transparency, inspection and adaptation. Sound familiar? It is the same learning loop as Lean Startup, applied to building.

scenes.label: Scrum events
scenes.title: The sprint: one goal, one to four weeks
scenes.center: Sprint: 1–4 weeks, one Sprint Goal, a usable increment

nodes.title: Planning
nodes.text: Why this sprint matters, what we can finish, and how.

nodes.title: Daily scrum
nodes.text: 15 minutes: progress towards the goal, and what blocks us.

nodes.title: Review
nodes.text: Show the increment to stakeholders; update the backlog.

nodes.title: Retro
nodes.text: Improve how we work in the next sprint.

beats.say: Everything happens inside the sprint: a fixed period of one to four weeks, with one sprint goal. It starts with sprint planning: why this sprint matters, what the team can finish, and how.
Every day, a fifteen-minute daily scrum: how are we progressing towards the goal, and what is blocking us?
At the end, the sprint review: the team shows the increment to stakeholders, and the backlog is updated with what they learned.
And the retrospective: how can we work better in the next sprint? Then the next sprint starts immediately.

scenes.label: Scrum artifacts
scenes.title: Each artifact has a commitment
rows: Where is the product going, and what is next?
What will we achieve in this sprint?
Is it really finished and usable?

beats.say: Since the 2020 Scrum Guide, each artifact comes with a commitment. The product backlog is ordered towards a product goal: where the product is going.
The sprint backlog is committed to a sprint goal: what we will achieve in this sprint.
And the increment must meet the definition of done. If it is not done, it is not part of the increment, and it is not shown in the review.

scenes.label: SDLC inside Scrum
scenes.title: Every sprint is a small SDLC

steps.title: Design and build
steps.text: Small slices, reviewed as you go.

steps.title: Test
steps.text: Tested before it counts as done.

beats.say: So where did the software development life cycle go? It did not disappear. It got smaller. Every sprint runs through all the phases. Planning becomes sprint planning.
Design and implementation happen every day, in small slices.
Testing is part of the definition of done, not a phase at the end.
Deployment produces a usable increment, ideally released to real users.
And maintenance and improvement come from the review and the retrospective. Seven phases, every few weeks, instead of once a year.

scenes.label: 03 · Make work visible
scenes.title: A Kanban board: To do, Doing, Done

beats.say: Agile teams make work visible on a board. Each column is a state of the work: backlog, to do, doing and done.
Each card is a user story or a task.
When a card is finished, it moves to done.
And only then does a new card enter doing. This is the key idea of Kanban: a work-in-progress limit. Here, no more than two cards in doing at a time. Stop starting, start finishing.

scenes.label: Scrum or Kanban?
scenes.title: Two ways to use the board
rows: Lead time and work in progress

beats.say: Scrum and Kanban both use boards, but differently. Scrum works in fixed sprints, with defined roles, and changes the plan between sprints.
Kanban is a continuous flow, with no required roles, where priorities can change at any time. Scrum measures velocity per sprint. Kanban measures lead time and limits work in progress.
Use Scrum to build a product towards goals. Use Kanban for support, operations, or any continuous flow of requests. Many teams mix both.

scenes.label: 04 · Tools
scenes.title: Trello: simple, visual boards

cards.title: Boards, lists, cards
cards.text: A board per project, a list per column, a card per task, with checklists, dates and members.

cards.title: Power-Ups and automation
cards.text: Add calendars, integrations and rules that move or update cards for you.

cards.title: Free for small teams
cards.text: Up to 10 collaborators per workspace on the free plan.

scenes.banner: Best for: student projects, small teams and simple Kanban boards.

beats.say: Now the tools. Trello is the simplest way to run a board. A board per project, a list per column, and a card per task, with checklists, due dates and members.
Power-Ups add calendars and integrations, and automation rules can move or update cards for you.
The free plan allows up to ten collaborators per workspace.
Trello is perfect for student projects, small teams and simple Kanban boards like the one we just saw.

scenes.label: Tools
scenes.title: Jira: Scrum and Kanban at scale

cards.title: Backlog and sprints
cards.text: Epics, stories and sub-tasks; estimate with story points and plan sprints by dragging.

cards.title: Boards and workflows
cards.text: Scrum and Kanban boards, with custom statuses and rules.

cards.title: Agile reports
cards.text: Burndown and velocity charts show progress and capacity.

cards.title: Free for small teams
cards.text: Up to 10 users on the free plan.

scenes.banner: Best for: software teams that run real sprints, track estimates and need reports.

beats.say: Jira, also from Atlassian, is built for Scrum. You organise work in epics, stories and sub-tasks, estimate them in story points, and plan sprints by dragging items from the backlog.
It has Scrum and Kanban boards with custom workflows.
And agile reports, like burndown and velocity charts, that show progress and the team's real capacity.
The free plan covers up to ten users.
Use Jira when a team runs real sprints, tracks estimates and needs reports.

scenes.label: In practice
scenes.title: Set up your project in six steps

steps.title: Create the board
steps.text: Scrum template in Jira, or a Trello board with lists.

steps.title: Write the backlog
steps.text: Epics and user stories, ordered by value.

steps.title: Estimate
steps.text: Story points or T-shirt sizes, as a team.

steps.title: Plan the sprint
steps.text: A sprint goal and the stories that achieve it.

steps.title: Review and retro
steps.text: Show the increment, update the backlog.

beats.say: Here is how to start your own project. Create the board: a Scrum project in Jira, or a Trello board with your lists.
Write the backlog: epics and user stories, ordered by value. Then estimate them as a team, in story points or T-shirt sizes.
Plan the first sprint: a sprint goal, and the stories that achieve it.
Run it every day on the board, respecting the work-in-progress limit. And close each sprint with a review and a retrospective that update the backlog.

scenes.label: Definition of done
scenes.title: When is a story really done?

beats.say: One last tool, and maybe the most important: a shared definition of done. Agree on it before the first sprint. A story is done when it meets its acceptance criteria, has been reviewed by a teammate, and its tests pass.
When it is deployed to a test environment, accepted by the product owner, and the documentation is updated. Not before.

scenes.label: Takeaway
scenes.text: Agile is a way of learning, not a tool.
scenes.sub: Go through the whole life cycle in short sprints, with clear roles and a visible board. Trello and Jira only make it visible.

beats.say: To sum up. The software development life cycle is always there. Agile runs it in short cycles, so you learn early and change cheaply.

Scrum gives you roles, events and artifacts. Kanban gives you flow and work-in-progress limits. Trello and Jira make the work visible. But the tool is not the method: what matters is a team that delivers, inspects and adapts, every sprint.
